title: From genes to everyday experience — a six-level teaching model
intro: Select any part to see what it does, what it connects to, and how strong each connection is. Switch on a medication overlay to see where each medicine is understood to act. The core parts are few; the complexity is in how they are regulated and how they differ between people.
note: Teaching model, not a diagnosis. Real systems involve hundreds of genes, many cell types and feedback loops. Solid = established mechanism · dashed = association in groups · dotted = hypothesis.

items.name: Many common variants
items.desc: Twin studies estimate heritability around 74%. Genome-wide studies find many common variants, each with a very small effect; 27 loci reached significance in the largest study, with 76 candidate genes enriched for expression in early brain development.

items.name: Rare variants
items.desc: Rare protein-truncating variants and copy-number changes add risk in some people. The 2023 study implicated SORCS3 through both common and rare variants.

items.name: Shared with other conditions
items.desc: An estimated 84–98% of ADHD-influencing variants are shared with other psychiatric conditions — one reason ADHD so often co-occurs with others, and why genes cannot diagnose an individual.

items.name: Tyrosine hydroxylase
items.desc: The enzyme that makes L-DOPA from tyrosine — the usual rate-limiting step in making dopamine and noradrenaline.

items.name: VMAT2 (vesicle loader)
items.desc: Pumps dopamine from the cell fluid into storage vesicles, ready for release. Amphetamines disturb this storage and redistribute dopamine into the cell fluid.

items.name: DAT (dopamine transporter)
items.desc: Recaptures released dopamine, ending its signal. Methylphenidate blocks it; amphetamines can reverse it so it pushes dopamine out.

items.name: NET (noradrenaline transporter)
items.desc: Recaptures noradrenaline — and in the prefrontal cortex, where DAT is sparse, much of the dopamine too. Atomoxetine blocks it.

items.name: MAO and COMT
items.desc: Enzymes that break dopamine and noradrenaline down inside and outside cells.

items.name: D1 and D2 receptors
items.desc: Receive the dopamine signal. D2 receptors on the releasing cell also act as a brake (autoreceptors), feeding back to reduce release.

items.name: Alpha-2A receptors
items.desc: Noradrenaline receptors in prefrontal cortex that strengthen task-relevant network signals. Guanfacine stimulates them.

items.name: Make
items.desc: Tyrosine → L-DOPA → dopamine (→ noradrenaline in noradrenergic cells).

items.name: Store
items.desc: Dopamine is packed into vesicles; unpacked dopamine is vulnerable to breakdown.

items.name: Release
items.desc: Vesicles release their contents when the cell fires. Amphetamines add a second, firing-independent release route.

items.name: Clear
items.desc: Transporters pull the signal back in; enzymes break it down. Most medicines act by slowing clearance or forcing release.

items.name: Self-tune
items.desc: Autoreceptors and adaptation adjust the system over time. Transporter levels appear to shift after stimulant exposure — which complicates brain-scan comparisons.

items.name: Prefrontal regulation
items.desc: Prefrontal cortex regulates attention, behaviour and emotion; imaging shows these regions less active, with weaker connections, in ADHD on average. Its function depends on finely tuned dopamine and noradrenaline levels.

items.name: Cortical maturation timing
items.desc: In 223 children with ADHD versus 223 controls, half of cortical points reached peak thickness by about 10.5 years versus 7.5 years — a delay most marked in prefrontal regions.

items.name: Subcortical volumes
items.desc: Across 23 sites, accumbens, amygdala, caudate, hippocampus and putamen were slightly smaller on average (effect sizes d −0.11 to −0.19), mainly in children; differences in adults were not significant. Medication did not explain them.

items.name: Reward pathway markers
items.desc: In 53 unmedicated adults, PET showed lower dopamine transporter and D2/D3 receptor binding in reward regions, correlating with inattention. But a meta-analysis found transporter levels lower in drug-naive and higher in previously medicated people — so findings depend on history.

items.name: Executive control
items.desc: Holding a goal, inhibiting distractions, switching and planning. Common-variant ADHD risk is associated with weaker performance on several executive measures.

items.name: Reward and motivation
items.desc: How strongly future or delayed outcomes drive effort now.

items.name: Arousal and state
items.desc: Matching alertness to the task — too little or too much both degrade control.

items.name: Starting tasks
items.desc: Knowing what to do and not being able to begin — one of the most commonly described ADHD difficulties.

items.name: Holding intentions
items.desc: Losing track of a plan between deciding and doing; forgetting why you entered a room.

items.name: Time awareness
items.desc: Under-estimating elapsed time and time needed; 'now' and 'not now' as the only two clocks.

items.name: Acting before deciding
items.desc: Speech or action running ahead of evaluation.

links.note: Risk genes are enriched for early brain development expression; the route to cortical timing is not demonstrated.
Common-variant risk is associated with midbrain dopaminergic neuron expression (Demontis 2023).
Individual rare-variant routes are mostly untested.
Whether transporter differences are a cause or an adaptation to past medication is unresolved (Fusar-Poli 2012).
Individual differences in vesicle storage capacity shaping stimulant response is a research question, not an established ADHD mechanism.

drugs.name: Methylphenidate
drugs.desc: Blocks dopamine and noradrenaline transporters, so released transmitter stays active longer. First-line in children and one of two first-line options in adults (NICE).

drugs.name: Amphetamines (dexamfetamine)
drugs.desc: Enter the terminal, disturb vesicle storage and run transporters in reverse, releasing dopamine and noradrenaline independent of firing; they also block reuptake. In adults' clinician-rated trials, amphetamines had the largest average symptom effect, with lower tolerability than placebo.

drugs.name: Lisdexamfetamine (Elvanse)
drugs.desc: An inactive prodrug absorbed intact and converted to d-amphetamine, mainly by red blood cells. Same active drug as dexamfetamine, delivered more gradually — a different exposure profile, not an identical one.

drugs.name: Atomoxetine
drugs.desc: Non-stimulant that blocks the noradrenaline transporter, raising noradrenaline and prefrontal dopamine.

drugs.name: Guanfacine
drugs.desc: Non-stimulant that stimulates alpha-2A receptors in prefrontal cortex, strengthening network signalling.
